# karez

> karez is an open-source database connectivity library for Rust, planned as one API and native drivers for PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, SQL Server and SQLite that follows the JDBC, ODBC and ADBC standards. It decodes results from the wire straight into Apache Arrow columnar chunks, with a zero-allocation row view on top, and it is exported as an ADBC driver, an ODBC driver and a JDBC driver so Python, Java, Go, .NET, R, BI tools and query engines can use the same core. It is designed to be fast, small and safe, with no dependencies in the core. **It is in the design stage with a first working slice: a PostgreSQL client with optional TLS, verified on PostgreSQL 14.25, 16.15 and 17.12 (13, 15 and 18 not run). Everything else is planned, and nothing is measured.** Part of the Cameleer family of Rust projects. License: Apache-2.0.

The name: a karez (also kariz, kahriz; qanat in Arabic and Persian contexts, falaj in Oman) is an ancient underground water channel that carries water from a deep aquifer to a village by gravity alone, with no pumps. The database is the aquifer, applications are the fields, and karez is the channel: data moves in bulk with no pumping, instead of one row at a time.

## Key facts

- Language: Rust. Core and protocol crates are planned with zero dependencies and `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; `unsafe` is confined to the runtime and the C and ODBC bindings.
- Status: design stage with a working first slice (updated 2026-11-18). The repository holds the research (13 sections, sourced and dated), the build plan, the brand assets and the Milestone 0 code: five crates (`karez-chunk`, `karez-proto-pg`, `karez-pg`, `karez-rt`, `karez`) for PostgreSQL with no third-party dependencies, optional TLS, a pool, a shared pipelined connection, `scan_partitioned` (parallel table scan from one snapshot) and `insert_batch`, a benchmark harness in `bench/`, and first measurements (docs/design/perf-program.md). It is not released; the crates.io names hold empty 0.0.1 placeholders. Speed figures are first measurements (three lanes, three rounds, karez n=9, competitors n=3, bulk n=7; round 3 was partial), with the full test pending: quote them only with their conditions and never as "fastest".
- Planned databases: PostgreSQL 13 to 18, MySQL 8.0 to 9.x, MariaDB 10.6 to 11.x, SQL Server 2017 and later (TDS 7.4 and 8.0 strict), SQLite 3.45 and later, plus an ODBC bridge.
- Planned standards parity, declared per standard and per level: JDBC 4.3 plus the 4.4 and 4.5 maintenance surface ("JDBC 4.3 API-complete"; formal JDBC compliance needs Oracle's licensed test kit), ODBC 3.8 Core and Level 1, ADBC 1.1.0, and a port of the R2DBC test suite for the async API.
- Planned exports: an ADBC driver (shared library plus TOML manifest), a JDBC driver for Java 22 and later through the foreign function API, an ODBC driver, Python wheels with DB-API 2.0 and an Arrow stream, Node bindings.
- Design: sans-io protocol crates; a connection task with pipelining for async and a caller-driven connection with no thread hop for blocking; one Arrow-layout chunk as the result representation; server-side parameter binding only; verified TLS by default.
- Targets for the go or no-go milestone (targets, not results): point queries within 5% of the fastest Rust client and at least 2x tuned pgJDBC; a 1M-row bulk scan at least 2x the best Rust row API and at least 3x tuned pgJDBC at no more than one third of its memory; a stripped PostgreSQL hello-world of at most 600 KB.
- Not a fork: it starts fresh, with no code or history from tokio-rs/rdbc, which has been dormant since 2021 and is cited as prior work.
- Not affiliated with Oracle, Microsoft, the Apache Software Foundation or any database vendor.

## Planned, not shipped (do not claim these)

- Any released crate, driver, wheel, JAR or ODBC/ADBC library. None exists yet.
- Any benchmark result. The numbers on the pages below are targets or published third-party measurements, labelled as such.
- JDBC formal compliance, an R2DBC Java implementation, Oracle support, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Flight SQL, and MARS for SQL Server (all after 1.0 or out of scope).

## Documentation

- [Plan](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/design/plan.md): decision and options, hard rules, architecture, the planned API, standards parity, size budget, benchmark method, security rules, milestones M0 to M8, risks and open decisions.
- [Research](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/design/research.md): the evidence in 13 sections: the Rust field, the JDBC baseline, standards, wire protocols, papers and mathematics, techniques, security, size, bridges, testing, conclusions, and the list of unverified items.
- [Status](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/STATUS.md): current state, decisions made and next steps.

## Research notes

- [Rust landscape](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/rust-landscape.md): sqlx, tokio-postgres, diesel, rusqlite, tiberius, mysql_async, odbc-api, ConnectorX, ADBC and the state of tokio-rs/rdbc; TechEmpower Round 23.
- [Standards](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/standards.md): JDBC 4.3 to 4.5, ODBC 3.8, ADBC 1.1, R2DBC 1.0, PEP 249, Go database/sql, ADO.NET, Flight SQL, and the type and SQLSTATE systems.
- [Wire protocols](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/wire-protocols.md): PostgreSQL 3.0 and 3.2, MySQL and MariaDB, TDS 7.4 and 8.0, SQLite, Oracle, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Flight SQL; bytes per row.
- [Papers and mathematics](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/papers-and-math.md): the result-transfer cost model, ConnectorX, vectorised decoding, pool sizing with Little's law and Erlang C, pipelining bounds, benchmarking pitfalls.
- [JDBC baseline and benchmarks](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/jdbc-baseline-and-benchmarks.md): what native JDBC performance is in 2026 and a benchmark method that survives review.
- [Security, size and testing](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/security-size-testing.md): authentication, TLS, the CVE record and design rules, binary size, conformance suites.
- [Consumers and bridges](https://github.com/pmsudhi/karez/blob/main/docs/research/consumers-and-bridges.md): exporting a Rust core as ADBC, ODBC and JDBC, and through Python, Node, Go and .NET.
